title: Surjectivity detected by restriction of finite continuous actions
statement:
Let $H$ and $G$ be profinite groups, meaning compact Hausdorff topological groups with a neighbourhood basis of the identity consisting of open normal subgroups. Let $h:H\to G$ be a continuous group homomorphism. For $T=G,H$, write $\mathrm{FinCont}(T)$ for the category of finite sets with left $T$-actions continuous for the discrete topology, and equivariant maps, as in the finite discrete continuous set convention of [def-pod-finite-continuous-module]. The restriction functor
$$\operatorname{Res}_h:\mathrm{FinCont}(G)\longrightarrow\mathrm{FinCont}(H),\qquad t\cdot_{\operatorname{Res}_h E}e=h(t)\cdot_E e,$$
acts as the identity on underlying functions. Then $h$ is surjective if and only if $\operatorname{Res}_h$ is fully faithful, that is, for every $E,D\in\mathrm{FinCont}(G)$ the map
$$\operatorname{Hom}_G(E,D)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_H(\operatorname{Res}_h E,\operatorname{Res}_h D)$$
is bijective.

source.place: Tag 0BN6, lemma-functoriality-galois-surjective, equivalence (1) with (2), and its proof for finite continuous group actions.

proof.text: Restriction preserves equivariance and is the identity on underlying functions, so it is faithful. If $h$ is surjective and $a:E\to D$ is $H$-equivariant, then for $g\in G$ choose $t\in H$ with $h(t)=g$. For every $e\in E$, $a(ge)=a(h(t)e)=h(t)a(e)=ga(e)$. Thus the same function is $G$-equivariant, proving fullness and hence full faithfulness. This includes empty actions. The action and morphism conventions are those of [def-pod-finite-continuous-module].

source.place: Tag 0BN6, lemma-functoriality-galois-surjective, proof of (1) implies (2), and final paragraph proving the converse using an open subgroup and its coset action.

proof.text: Conversely assume full faithfulness and suppose $h$ is not onto. Put $K=h(H)$, a subgroup since $h$ preserves multiplication and inverses. By [lem-dl-a1-compact-hausdorff-closed-map] applied to $h:H\to G$, the image $K$ is closed: the source is compact, the target Hausdorff and $h$ continuous. Choose $g\in G\setminus K$.

source.place: Tag 0BN6, lemma-functoriality-galois-surjective, proof of (1) implies (2), and final paragraph proving the converse using an open subgroup and its coset action.

proof.text: The open set $g^{-1}(G\setminus K)=\{x\in G:gx\notin K\}$ is a neighbourhood of $1$. By the normal-subgroup neighbourhood basis in the hypothesis choose an open normal $N\leq G$ inside it, so $gN\cap K=\varnothing$. Set $U=KN$. Normality of $N$ makes this a subgroup: $(kn)(k_1 n_1)=kk_1(k_1^{-1}nk_1)n_1\in KN$, and $(kn)^{-1}=k^{-1}(kn^{-1}k^{-1})\in KN$. It contains $K$ and is open, being the union of translates $kN$ for $k\in K$; translation and its inverse are continuous by the group axioms. If $g=kn$ belonged to $KN$, then $k=gn^{-1}\in gN\cap K$, a contradiction. Hence $U$ is a proper open subgroup containing $K$.

source.place: Tag 0BN6, lemma-functoriality-galois-surjective, proof of (1) implies (2), and final paragraph proving the converse using an open subgroup and its coset action.

proof.text: Apply [lem-dl-a1-open-subgroup-finite-cosets] to this $U$. It gives a finite discrete continuous $G$-action $M=G/U$ by left multiplication, without requiring $U$ normal. The coset $U\in M$ is fixed by $H$, because $h(H)=K\subseteq U$. Therefore the function $b:*\to\operatorname{Res}_h M$ with $b(*)=U$ is $H$-equivariant, where $*$ is the singleton with trivial action. Both $M$ and $*$ are objects of the finite-action category, with singleton and equivariant-map conventions from [def-pod-finite-continuous-module].

source.place: Tag 0BN6, lemma-functoriality-galois-surjective, proof of (1) implies (2), and final paragraph proving the converse using an open subgroup and its coset action.

proof.text: Fullness lifts $b$ to a $G$-equivariant map $a:*\to M$. Restriction is the identity on functions, so $a(*)=U$. Equivariance says $xU=x\cdot a(*)=a(x\cdot *)=a(*)=U$ for every $x\in G$. Equality of these left cosets means $x\in U$, contradicting $g\notin U$ from step 3. Thus $h$ is onto. Together with step 1 this proves the equivalence.
